paper.title: Hemispheric contributions to praxis: imitation of gestures and pantomime of tool use following left and right hemisphere damage

shots.narration: After a stroke, some people can still move their arm, yet they can no longer show how to use a familiar tool.

shots.narration: This is apraxia: a breakdown not of strength, but of the brain's plan for skilled movement. It shows up two ways. Copying a gesture you're shown,
shots.klingPrompt: Cinematic documentary footage, two people seated across a small table, one hand demonstrating a simple hand gesture while the other person's hand tries to copy it and falters mid-movement, close on the two hands, locked-off camera, soft even clinical light, cool palette with warm skin tones, shallow depth of field, photoreal, 16:9

shots.narration: and miming how to use a tool from memory. Do these two abilities live in the same place in the brain?
shots.onscreen: Imitation and pantomime — one brain system, or two?
shots.klingPrompt: Cinematic documentary footage, an older adult seated, miming the act of turning a key in mid-air on command, the wrist rotation stalling and the fingers losing the shape of the grip, the camera pushing in slowly toward the hand, soft clinical light, cool palette with warm skin tones, shallow depth of field, photoreal, 16:9

shots.narration: To find out, researchers studied 78 stroke survivors, some with left-brain damage, some with right, and mapped exactly where each stroke had struck.
Everyone took two standard tests: one for imitating gestures, one for pantomiming tool use.

shots.narration: Their brain scans were aligned to a common template, so damage could be compared, voxel by voxel, against performance.

shots.narration: The maps revealed something striking. The regions where damage broke pantomime were mostly not the regions where damage broke imitation. Two different territories.
And the two hemispheres were organized differently.
shots.klingPrompt: Cinematic medical 3D render, a whole human brain viewed from above, the camera tracking slowly from the left hemisphere across the midline to the right hemisphere, the cortical folds catching soft light, dark clinical void, deep blue and teal palette with a faint warm rim, photoreal subsurface scattering, shallow depth of field, 16:9

shots.narration: In the left brain, about a quarter of the critical spots mattered for both skills, meeting along a major white-matter highway. In the right brain, almost none did. There, damage tended to knock out just one skill or the other.
That matters for recovery. If imitation and pantomime can break separately, therapy can target the specific skill a person has lost,

shots.narration: And it overturns an old assumption, that praxis is purely left-brained. Both hemispheres shape how we turn intention into skilled action.
